# Remote work is quietly slowing down junior developers

Junior developers grow by osmosis. They overhear a senior engineer talking through a production incident, they watch how a tech lead pushes back on a vague ticket, they absorb a hundred small judgments that nobody would ever think to write down. Remote work cut that channel, and three years in, engineering managers are starting to see the bill.

I noticed it first in code review turnaround. In the office, a junior who got a confusing review comment would swivel a chair and ask. On Slack, the same junior sits on the comment for half a day, drafts a reply, deletes it, and finally schedules a call for Thursday. The feedback loop that used to take ninety seconds now takes two days, and learning speed is mostly a function of feedback-loop length.

But the picture is more complicated than "office good, remote bad." Hybrid schedules were supposed to fix this, and mostly they haven't, because hybrid without coordination is just remote with commuting. If the senior engineers come in on Tuesday and the juniors on Wednesday, nobody learns anything from anybody. The companies that make hybrid work treat office days as a scheduling problem: whole teams in on the same days, calendars cleared for pairing.

Of course, the office itself is a cost center, and this is where the conversation usually goes sideways. A mid-size company pays somewhere between €8,000 and €15,000 per desk per year in a major European city once you count rent, fit-out, and services. Finance teams have noticed. A lot of the return-to-office push has nothing to do with mentorship and everything to do with justifying leases signed in 2019. That's worth being honest about, because employees can smell the difference between "we want you to grow" and "we prepaid for this building."

There's also a hiring angle that doesn't get enough attention. Remote-first companies can recruit from anywhere, which transformed the talent market for smaller cities. A competent developer in Porto or Leipzig no longer has to choose between local salaries and relocation. Companies that mandate office attendance are effectively cutting their candidate pool by 90% and paying the metropolitan salary premium for the privilege. For some roles that trade is defensible; for most, it's inertia.

Which brings up the employer-brand question: the companies loudest about returning to the office tend to be the ones with the weakest engineering brands, because strong brands don't need leverage — people already want to work there. Watch what the companies everyone wants to join are doing, not what the loudest CEOs are saying.

So what should a team actually do about the juniors? Some options: structured pairing rotations, dedicated "office hours" channels where questions are expected rather than apologized for, and recording senior engineers' debugging sessions. Each of these rebuilds part of the osmosis channel. None of them is as good as sitting next to someone, but together they close maybe most of the gap, and they have the advantage of working for the remote employees you're going to have anyway.

The real lesson might be that companies never understood where junior growth came from in the first place. The office provided mentorship by accident. Remote work just revealed that nobody was doing it on purpose.
